The first step in this process is to gather datasets from different sources. Social networking networks and online news portals might offer datasets for this. Each dataset presents unique challenges and features which ensure a comprehensive evaluation of the models' applications in real-world scenarios. Text preparation has a crucial role in enhancing the models' capacity to distinguish bogus news. To do this, in order to extract valuable information from the text input, operations like encoding, stemming, and stop word removal must be carried out. Moreover, the textual data can be represented in a way suitable for machine learning models by using techniques like word embeddings of Term FrequencyInverse Document Frequency (Aphiwongsophon et al., 2018). Decision trees can be trained on several subsets of the dataset using an advanced ensemble learning method called Random Forest. The collective wisdom of these trees reduces overfitting and strengthens the model's robustness, making it perfect for spotting misleading information. Naive Bayes is a probabilistic classifier that assumes feature independence. It is a valuable addition to the model collection since, despite its simplicity, it often achieves good results in text categorization tasks. Nearest Neighbour uses similarity measures to classify instances. By considering the proximity of data points in a feature space, it can identify trends in the dataset and identify fake news more effectively. A good linear model for tasks requiring binary classification is logistic regression. It can be used to simulate the chance that a news piece is fraudulent and produce results that are easy to grasp. The most effective hyperplane to divide classes is found using the complex classification method known as Support Vector Machine (SVM). Text classification makes good use of SVM's high-dimensional feature space handling capabilities. These models are systematically applied in order to develop a flexible and precise false news detection system. This is due to the fact that they use preprocessed datasets from various sources. It is necessary to consistently assess these models and make refinements where necessary. This will help better the detecting of changing patters across various datasets. This in turn will assist in identifying the spread of false information. Developing methods for automatically detecting false information is crucial to reducing the harmful impacts of fake news. The main place to accomplish this is on social media. Because it is convenient and inexpensive to manufacture, fake news is produced in large quantities, which makes automated identification essential. Machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI) have emerged as viable remedies for this issue (Villela et al., 2023). Research evaluating several approaches to false news detection have evaluated the performance of each algorithm across several datasets. A couple of the challenges include the need for trustworthy models that perform well with various types of news and dataset bias. Moreover, the employment of advanced pre-trained language models such as BERT, ELECTRA, and ELMo has shown promise in improving detection accuracy (Shu et al., 2017). One way to detect how effective machine learning algorithms are can be done by thoroughly analyzing them. This covers both conventional (SVM, LR, Decision Tree, Naive Bayes, k-NN) and deep learning (CNN, LSTM, Bi-LSTM, C-LSTM, HAN, Conv-HAN) models. As a global platform for real-time discussion, social media platforms have been instrumental in the dissemination of false information. Because users can search for tweets about particular subjects using the platform's streaming API, it is an invaluable tool for researchers examining the mechanics of fake news on social media platforms (Ahmed et al., 2020). The scientific community has realized that in order to categorize news as authentic or fraudulent, real-time data extraction from social media platforms and analyzing them later using machine learning algorithms are required. Methodology The detection of fake news in this project was done in three steps. Initially, the data was collected and cleaned, before being preprocessed in the next steps. ● Removing Numbers: The removal of numbers from the text is essential to eliminate numerical information that may not contribute to the classification of news types. It simplifies the text, focusing on linguistic patterns rather than numerical values. ● Removing Punctuation: Punctuation removal streamlines the text further by eliminating symbols that do not carry significant meaning in natural language processing. This step aids in reducing noise and simplifying the language representation. ● Removing Special Characters: The removal of special characters while retaining alphanumeric characters and spaces ensures that only relevant textual information is considered. This step aims to create a cleaner, more standardized representation of the text. ● Removing English Stopwords: Stopwords, common words like "and," "the," and "is," were removed to focus on more meaningful terms. Eliminating stopwords reduces noise in the data and emphasizes words with higher semantic value. ● Stemming: The application of stemming involves reducing words to their root forms, aiding in normalization and capturing core meanings. The Porter Stemmer from NLTK is a popular choice for this task. ● Tokenization: Tokenization is a process that breaks down the text into individual units, such as words or phrases. Features Extraction, Model Training and Results The combined dataset was subjected to feature extraction, model training, and evaluation in the last stage of the investigation. The objective was to create a reliable system that could identify, using specific textual characteristics, between news that was authentic and that was not. The procedure was choosing the news_type column to be the target variable (Y) and the text column to be the feature variable (X). Two feature extraction programmes, CountVectorizer and TfidfTransformer, were used to convert the textual data into a format appropriate for machine learning models. 1. CountVectorizer: This straightforward but effective tool creates a matrix of token counts from several text sources. A document is represented by each row in the matrix, and a unique token from the corpus is represented by each column. The values in the matrix show how frequently each token appears in the corresponding documents. By converting language into numerical characteristics, machine learning algorithms are able to handle and evaluate textual input more efficiently. 2. TfidfTransformer: Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency is a statistic that can be used to determine a word's significance inside a document in relation to a group of documents. TfidfTransformer is used to further enhance the feature representation after CountVectorizer. Tokens

are given weights according to how frequently they occur within a particular text and how rarely they occur within the corpus as a whole. This normalization highlights the value of unique terms in each document while lessening the influence of common ones. After the extraction of features, the data was processed and prepared for model training. Although the precise algorithms were not stated, five supervised machine learning classification algorithms were used. These algorithms were used to identify trends in the text data's feature representations and forecast the kind of news—genuine or fraudulent. The labelled dataset, in which each instance was connected to a particular news genre, was presented to the algorithms as part of the model training process. During this training phase, the algorithms discovered the patterns that were present in the text and how they related to the different kinds of news. Lastly, performance indicators were used to assess the trained models, with accuracy being emphasised as the main metric. After that, a number of techniques, including Support Vector Machine, Random Forest, Naïve Bayes, Nearest Neighbour, and Logistic Regression, were used to assess the models. Next, the algorithms were ranked based on F-1 support, accuracy, precision, and recall. With an 81% success rate in properly detecting news genres, the Support Vector Machine (SVM) model proved to be the most accurate among the tested models. Although Logistic Regression was the least dependable approach, Naive Bayes also produced extremely accurate findings (Jain et al., 2019). This shows that SVM performed better than other algorithms in differentiating between bogus and real news in the provided dataset, based on the chosen textual features and the preprocessing processes. The accuracy statistic highlights the SVM model's dependability in this situation by displaying the percentage of successfully classified occurrences. Future Research When detecting and analyzing if news was fake or real, an assumption was made that all news over 0.5 spam score are real, whilst the others are fake. This assumption led to the majority of the samples being skewed towards the real samples. If some other factor, other than 0.5 would be taken, it would have led to completely different results. For example, using a higher factor would mean more fake results, while vice versa, a lower factor would mean more real results. To counter this some other metric besides spam score can also be used in order to derive results. Another assumption made was that the independent feature (X) in this study was ‘text’, while the target variable (Y) was news_type.
